description: Team NEXUS combines expertise in advanced mathematical physics, full-stack web development, and algorithmic problem-solving. With a rigorous background from a specialized STEM academy and top finishes in national coding competitions, our team is uniquely equipped to handle complex astrometric math and custom FITS data processing. We leverage extensive experience in Node.js, 3D modeling, and WebGL to seamlessly render massive datasets.
summary:
We developed NEXUS, a web platform that transforms NASA's SPHEREx raw infrared images and ESA's GAIA data into an interactive sky map accessible directly in the browser, requiring no downloads or coding experience.

This directly addresses the challenge by enabling anyone to easily explore the massive 102-band dataset and track shifting celestial objects. NEXUS features three primary views: a full sky map, a SPHEREx photo analyzer with time-lapse capabilities (Co-add, Blink, and Difference modes), and an interactive 3D map powered by GAIA, visualizing 321,302 stars at their true distances. To process this, we built a custom FITS file reader and implemented scientific algorithms to measure motion and parallax using GAIA's precise astrometry.

NEXUS is important because it bridges the gap between complex raw scientific archives and the general public. It offers a "Standard" mode featuring an AI guide (NEXUS-7) for beginners, and an "Advanced" mode for researchers to analyze spectrums, measure light curves, and conduct blind searches for new moving objects using 100% real, open-source data.
details:
NEXUS is a browser-based web platform that transforms raw infrared images from NASA's SPHEREx telescope and astrometric data from ESA's GAIA into an interactive, explorable universe. It operates entirely in the browser without requiring any downloads, coding knowledge, or a traditional backend database—fetching and rendering 100% real scientific data on the fly.

NEXUS features three primary views:

  • Sky Map: A comprehensive view of the SPHEREx all-sky map, allowing users to zoom from a macro view down to a single star, with tools to cross-reference against other surveys (2MASS, AllWISE, DSS2).
  • SPHEREx Photo Analyzer: A time-lapse analyzer for specific coordinates featuring Co-add, Blink, Difference, and vs. Median modes to visually detect moving or changing objects over time.
  • 3D Star Map: An interactive 3D visualization of 321,302 GAIA stars within a 100-parsec radius. Users can hit "Play" to simulate stellar motion 50,000 years into the future based on their true measured velocities.

Every object includes a "Star Card" detailing its distance, temperature, size relative to the Sun, and its real path across the sky for 2024–2030.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We built NEXUS with a focus on performance and native capabilities:

  • Core Logic: Pure, framework-free vanilla JavaScript to ensure maximum speed when processing large datasets.
  • Graphics: Three.js for the 3D map and Earth models, and WebGL for rendering accurate star models.
  • Backend/Infrastructure: Vercel serverless functions to establish direct, secure connections to scientific archives.
  • Data Sources: NASA/IPAC IRSA (for live ADQL queries of SPHEREx DR1 FITS files), ESA Gaia DR3, and SIMBAD + Sesame (CDS) for object classifications and temperatures.
  • Custom Tooling: We wrote a custom FITS file reader from scratch that handles World Coordinate System (WCS) and SIP distortion, translating every pixel to exact Right Ascension and Declination (RA/Dec) coordinates.

How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider?

Our biggest creative challenge was handling massive astronomical datasets in a consumer browser. Instead of relying on a pre-packaged database, we engineered a pipeline that reads open scientific archives in real-time. For the GAIA data, we pre-processed the 321,302 stars into highly compact binary files to ensure seamless 3D rendering.

We also had to consider the realities of space photography. We built custom scientific algorithms, including an image co-adding technique designed specifically to filter out cosmic rays so they aren't falsely identified as moving objects. We also implemented least-squares methods to calculate motion and parallax accurately. To validate our math, we ran a simulation against Barnard’s Star, successfully recovering its true GAIA velocity (10.393 arcseconds/year) with an accuracy of 0.2%.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

NEXUS bridges the gap between raw, complex astronomical data and the public. To maximize its impact, we designed two distinct user experiences:

  • Standard Mode: Tailored for students and the general public, featuring "NEXUS-7," an AI guide that greets beginners and explains what they are looking at in simple terms.
  • Advanced Mode: Built for researchers, offering tools to analyze 102-band spectrums (0.75–5.0 micrometers), generate light curves, measure astrometric motion, export CSV/JSON files, and conduct blind searches for new solar system objects by cross-referencing SIMBAD and AllWISE.

By democratizing this data, NEXUS empowers anyone—from a curious middle schooler to a seasoned astrophysicist—to participate in decoding the shifting universe.
